content.title: About
content.content: Asparagus is the young shoot of the plant Asparagus officinalis. Frozen asparagus cooked with oil is a ready‑to‑eat product that retains most nutrients and its characteristic tender flavor. It is convenient for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the earliest cultivated vegetables, grown for over 2,000 years.
In the United States it is often called the “queen of spring” because of its seasonal appearance.
Freezing preserves up to 90 % of B‑vitamins and vitamin C when the product is flash‑frozen after harvest.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin K.
Asparagus contains aromatic compounds that give it its distinctive scent.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate supports cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A serving provides about 20 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Asparagus provides glutathione, vitamin C and vitamin E, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in asparagus promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The ready‑made product may contain added salt; people with hypertension should check sodium levels.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible persons.

items.title: Added oil
items.content: Since the product is already cooked in oil, total fat intake should be considered.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen asparagus in a skillet, microwave, or steamer. Serve as a side dish, add to salads, pasta, omelets, or incorporate into vegetable mixes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C in the original packaging. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef and noodles with gravy is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of tender beef pieces, boiled noodles, and a savory meat gravy. It is typically served hot as a main course in cafeterias or as a quick dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is popular in Eastern European and Asian cuisines where noodles are often paired with meat sauces.
Traditionally the beef is slow‑cooked to become tender and juicy.
The gravy is usually made from beef stock, cream, or tomato base, giving the dish a rich flavor.
Noodles are usually short (spaghetti, fettuccine) or egg‑based, which helps them hold the sauce.
The meal can be frozen and reheated in a microwave or on the stovetop for convenience.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies B12, B6 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates from noodles
items.content: Noodles deliver complex carbohydrates for a quick energy boost.

items.title: Collagen in the gravy
items.content: Meat‑based gravy contains collagen that may benefit joint and skin health.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Beef and meat‑based gravies can be high in saturated fat, so people with cardiovascular concerns should consume in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Gravy often contains added salt; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat‑based noodles contain gluten, making the dish unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial contamination; keep the product refrigerated and reheat promptly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the dish in a microwave or on the stovetop until it reaches at least 75 °C. It can be enjoyed on its own or paired with a vegetable side such as broccoli or carrots.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at ≤ 4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in an airtight container at −18 °C for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-ns-as-to.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, skin removed

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh without skin are cuts of poultry meat from which the outer skin has been removed. They are high in protein, low in fat, and suitable for a variety of cooking methods such as boiling, baking, grilling, and stewing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Skin‑less chicken contains roughly half the calories of the same cut with skin.
Drumsticks and thighs are the juiciest parts of the bird because they have more muscle fibers and connective tissue.
These cuts are featured in classic dishes worldwide, from French coq au vin to Asian teriyaki chicken.
When cooked properly without skin, chicken retains a good amount of B‑vitamins.
Skin‑less meat is easier to digest for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑gram serving provides about 20 grams of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin cuts saturated fat dramatically, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: phosphorus and selenium
items.content: Phosphorus is important for bone health, while selenium offers antioxidant protection.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Protein and zinc in chicken help strengthen the immune response.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals can be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content in marinades
items.content: Pre‑marinated cuts can be high in salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Overeating
items.content: Even skin‑less chicken is calorie‑dense; large portions can contribute to excess caloric intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skin‑less chicken is versatile: grill it, bake it, steam it, or braise it. Cut into cubes for soups, add to salads, roast with herbs and spices, or simmer in sauces. When baking, covering with foil helps prevent drying out.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pieces in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in airtight bags at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Dessert dip is a sweet, creamy topping designed to accompany ice cream, fruit, pancakes and other desserts. It is usually made from cream, sugar and flavorings such as vanilla, caramel or berries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dessert dips are often used in restaurants to create visual contrast with the main dessert.
There are more than 30 flavor variations: chocolate, caramel, berry, nut and others.
In the United States, cheese‑based dips like cream‑cheese berry sauce are popular.
Traditional French "crème de fruit" is made from fresh fruit, sugar and lemon juice.
In Japan, a sweet rice‑paste dip called "mochi" is commonly served with desserts.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cream base provides calcium, which is essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Some versions are fortified with vitamin D, helping the body absorb calcium.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Contains easily digestible sugars that can quickly replenish energy after physical activity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The dairy base can cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to milk may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip in small portions alongside a dessert, drizzling it over ice cream, pancakes, waffles or fresh fruit. It can also be used as a filling for cupcakes and rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip refrigerated at 2 °C–4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, it is usually good for 5–7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.

ice-cream-cone-soft-serve-chocolate.title: Ice Cream Cone, Soft Serve, Chocolate

content.title: About
content.content: Soft‑serve chocolate ice cream in a crunchy waffle cone is a classic treat featuring creamy ice cream coated with a thin chocolate glaze and served in a crisp cone. Portion size: 450 ml.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first ice‑cream cone was introduced in the United States in the early 1900s.
Chocolate glaze often contains cocoa butter, which gives it a glossy, snap‑crisp finish.
Soft‑serve is typically served at about –6 °C, making it lighter and airier than regular ice cream.
In some countries the cones are decorated with nuts, sprinkles, or caramel drizzle.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream used in the recipe are rich in vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from cocoa
items.content: Chocolate glaze contains flavonoids that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large servings can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains dairy, which may cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Allergy to nuts or soy emulsifiers
items.content: Chocolate glaze may contain nuts or soy lecithin, potential allergens for some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve immediately after preparation to keep the cone crunchy and the ice cream soft. Optionally garnish with sprinkles, fresh berries, or an extra drizzle of chocolate sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18 °C for no more than 2 weeks. Avoid repeated thawing to preserve the texture of the soft‑serve.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-made-with-mayonn.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with mayonnaise is a popular dish often served at picnics, family lunches, and holiday tables. The basic ingredients are cooked pasta, mayonnaise, vegetables (such as peas, carrots, cucumbers) and seasonings. Its simplicity and rich flavor make it a favorite in many countries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The pasta salad originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient picnic food.
Short-shaped pasta (rotini, penne, fusilli) is traditionally used because it holds the dressing well.
Regional variations add different ingredients: in Russia peas and carrots are common, while in Italy olives and Parmesan are added.
Mayonnaise can be substituted with yogurt or sour cream for a lighter version.
The salad keeps well in the fridge for 3‑4 days, but tastes best within the first 24 hours.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides energy through complex carbohydrates that are released slowly into the bloodstream.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Added vegetables (carrots, peas, cucumbers) enrich the salad with vitamins A, C, K and potassium.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Pasta and optional additions such as boiled chicken or eggs increase the protein content.

items.title: Probiotics (when using yogurt)
items.content: Replacing part of the mayo with natural yogurt introduces beneficial bacteria.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Peas and carrots add fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise is rich in saturated fats and calories; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Leaving the salad at room temperature for more than 2 hours can allow harmful bacteria to multiply.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Store‑bought mayo often contains a lot of salt; low‑sodium versions are better for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Regular pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives should be used for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side dish, alongside meat or fish, or use it as a filling for sandwiches and wraps. It travels well in a cooler or sealed container for picnics. Before serving, garnish with fresh herbs, paprika, or grated cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Stir before serving as the mayo may settle. Consume within 3‑4 days; discard if it develops an off‑odor or visible mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Mixed nuts with peanuts, salted is a blend of roasted peanuts, cashews, almonds, hazelnuts and other nuts, lightly salted to enhance flavor. The nuts provide a crunchy texture, aromatic scent and a subtle salty note, making them an ideal snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts are technically legumes, not true nuts.
Mixed nut blends are popular in sports nutrition for their high protein and healthy fat content.
A small amount of salt can amplify the perception of sweetness in nuts.
Nuts in the blend are often roasted in oil with spices, giving them a distinctive aroma.
Portion‑controlled packets make it easy to manage serving sizes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The blend provides plant‑based protein essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids support heart health and help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts and other nuts supply niacin, thiamine and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Magnesium, phosphorus and zinc from the nuts support muscle function, bone health and the immune system.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in the nuts promotes intestinal motility and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Tree nut and peanut allergy
items.content: People with allergies to nuts or peanuts may experience severe reactions when consuming the blend.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The mix is calorie‑dense, so portion control is important, especially on weight‑management diets.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Excessive salt intake can raise blood pressure; individuals with hypertension should limit consumption.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole nuts can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the mixed nuts as a standalone snack, sprinkle them over salads, yogurt, muesli, or incorporate them into baked goods. For extra aroma, briefly toast the nuts in a dry pan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Pakora is a popular Indian snack consisting of deep‑fried balls made from chickpea (gram) flour, vegetables and spices. The batter becomes crisp on the outside while staying soft inside, and the flavor is aromatic, mildly spicy and savory.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pakoras are a common street‑food across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
Traditional batter is made from chickpea flour, which is gluten‑free and high in protein.
There are many variations: onion, spinach, eggplant, seafood and even sweet fruit pakoras.
They are usually served with tamarind chutney or mint yogurt dip.
In some regions they are prepared during fasting periods because they contain no dairy.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpea flour provides about 20 % protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Chickpeas release glucose slowly, helping blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: When fried in vegetable oil, pakoras acquire a modest amount of monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Spices such as turmeric, cumin and coriander have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: People allergic to chickpeas or other legumes may react to pakoras.

items.title: High fat content from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying makes pakoras calorie‑dense and high in fat.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

items.title: Spice irritation
items.content: Strong spices may upset sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pakoras are served hot, typically with tamarind chutney, mint yogurt or tomato sauce. They can be enjoyed as a snack on their own or as part of a larger meal such as a biryani.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pakoras in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them; reheat in the oven before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter is a spread made from roasted ground peanuts (Arachis hypogaea), sometimes with salt, sugar, or oil. It has a thick, creamy or crunchy texture and a rich nutty flavor. It is spread on bread and toast and added to smoothies, porridge, baked goods, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, the peanut is a legume, not a true nut.
Peanut butter is very popular in the United States, where it is often eaten in sandwiches.
In natural peanut butter, the oil can collect on top, so it needs stirring.
Peanut butter comes smooth and crunchy, with bits of peanut.
Peanuts are the basis of African peanut stews and the Asian satay sauce.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides protein and helps you feel full for longer.

items.title: Contains unsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in peanuts is mono- and polyunsaturated.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contains magnesium and niacin
items.content: These nutrients support muscle and nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut allergy can be very severe, up to anaphylaxis; peanut butter is strictly off limits for people with this allergy.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Peanut butter is high in calories, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Additives in the ingredients
items.content: Some peanut butters contain added sugar, salt, and palm or hydrogenated oil.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Thick peanut butter can cause choking in small children, so it should be spread in a thin layer.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread peanut butter on bread and toast, or add it to oatmeal, yogurt, smoothies, pancakes, baked goods, and sauces, or serve it with apple or banana. A serving is one to two tablespoons. It is best to choose peanut butter with only peanuts and a little salt in the ingredients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peanut butter in a closed jar in a cool, dark place. After opening, natural peanut butter is better kept in the refrigerator so the oil does not turn rancid, and stirred before use. Discard peanut butter that smells rancid or is moldy.

peas-and-carrots-fresh-cooked-fat-added.title: Peas and carrots, fresh, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots are popular vegetables often combined in cooking. In this version they are fresh, boiled and prepared with added fat, which enhances flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas belong to the legume family and are rich in plant protein, while carrots are root vegetables high in beta‑carotene.
Traditionally in Russian cuisine peas and carrots are cooked together in soups and stews.
A small amount of vegetable oil increases the bioavailability of carotenoids from carrots.
The combination provides a broad spectrum of amino acids, complementing each other.
Both vegetables can be stored in the refrigerator for up to a week, but are best enjoyed fresh.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A to support vision and immunity.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Added vegetable fat (e.g., olive oil) supplies monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Both vegetables contain fiber that promotes healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Carotenoids and flavonoids in carrots and peas help combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Excessive fat intake
items.content: Too much added fat raises the calorie density of the dish.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions of peas can cause gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Carrots contain modest amounts of oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stones in predisposed individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish, add to salads, soups, or stews. Garnish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon juice for brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in a pan with a little oil to retain texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry pie is a dessert made with a tender crust filled with fresh or canned strawberries, often complemented by a buttery cream or custard sauce. It offers a sweet‑tart berry flavor and a crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberries are considered a symbol of summer and are frequently used in festive desserts.
Traditional English strawberry pie is often served with a mint sauce that highlights the berries' aroma.
In the United States, the “Strawberry Shortcake” version layers strawberries over a biscuit base with whipped cream.
Strawberry pie is commonly served chilled to keep the berries firm and the filling fresh.
Gluten‑free versions replace the crust with almond or oat flour.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Strawberries provide a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and anthocyanins in strawberries help combat free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fruit adds dietary fiber that promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The berry filling adds sweetness without many calories, making the pie lighter than many other desserts.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Strawberries are a good source of potassium, important for blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Strawberry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to strawberries, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Strawberry pies often contain added sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If non‑organic berries are used, pesticide residues may be present; washing or choosing organic fruit is recommended.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity of strawberries can irritate a sensitive stomach in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie in slices, often topped with whipped cream, ice cream, or a mint sauce. It can be enjoyed warm or chilled. For a lighter touch, add fresh berries on top.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pie refrigerated, covered with plastic wrap, for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze individual portions in airtight containers for up to 2 months. Allow it to come to room temperature briefly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Rutabaga, also known as swede or yellow turnip, is a root vegetable from the Brassicaceae family. Raw rutabaga has a firm, slightly sweet flesh, a crisp texture and a mildly bitter undertone. It is often used in salads, quick pickles, or as a crunchy addition to fresh dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rutabaga is a hybrid of cabbage and turnip that originated in Scandinavia.
Unlike many root vegetables, it can be stored in a cool place for up to six months.
It contains higher levels of glucosinolates than most Brassica vegetables, giving it a distinctive aroma.
In Japan, thinly sliced raw rutabaga is used in a traditional dish called "tsunaka" where it is pickled in vinegar.
The leafy tops are edible and rich in vitamins.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Rutabaga provides a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Its fiber content promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in electrolyte balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Raw rutabaga has a low energy density, making it a suitable choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: High in glucosinolates
items.content: These compounds may support detoxification processes and offer protection against certain cancers.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to members of the Brassicaceae family, including rutabaga.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Rutabaga contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: May cause digestive discomfort in large amounts
items.content: The high fiber level can lead to gas and bloating if consumed excessively.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice raw rutabaga thinly for salads, add it to fresh vegetable mixes, quick‑pickle it in vinegar, or use it as a crunchy garnish for fish and meat dishes. Be sure to wash it thoroughly before eating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rutabaga in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp cloth. Properly stored, it stays fresh for 2–3 weeks. Remove any damaged roots to prevent spoilage of the rest.
